plan.outcome7: By day 7 you'll be able to open a demat and trading account with a SEBI-registered broker, place a limit order for 1 share of a Nifty 50 company, read its price, market cap and P/E on a quote page, explain in one line why its price moved that day, and work out the tax you'd owe if you sold it.
plan.horizon14: Later, around day 14: you could compare two companies in the same sector using five numbers and say which you'd rather own and why.
plan.horizon28: Later, around day 28: you could have a written monthly plan splitting money between an index fund SIP and single shares, and one month of sticking to it.

picture.name: One big organised bazaar
picture.line: The Indian stock market is one huge organised bazaar: each company is a shop, a share is a tiny slice of ownership in one shop, and SEBI is the inspector who keeps the stalls honest.

chapters.title: A share is a slice of a shop
chapters.covers: What you actually own when you buy 1 share, and why its price moves every second: more buyers than sellers pushes it up, more sellers than buyers pushes it down.
chapters.outcome: You can explain in one line why a share's price rose or fell today using buyers and sellers, not headlines.
chapters.hook: Buy one share and you legally own a sliver of a company. What exactly did you buy?

chapters.title: The two bazaars and their price boards
chapters.covers: NSE and BSE are the two exchanges (the market buildings), open 9:15 am to 3:30 pm Monday to Friday; Nifty 50 and Sensex are price boards for the 50 and 30 biggest shops; SEBI is the inspector.
chapters.outcome: You can read 'Nifty closed 0.8% down' and say what it does and does not tell you about the 50 companies behind it.
chapters.hook: The Sensex is just 30 companies. So why does the whole country watch it?

chapters.title: Your three accounts
chapters.covers: Bank account holds your money, trading account places orders through a broker, demat account is the locker (with NSDL or CDSL) that holds your shares; what KYC with PAN and Aadhaar means and what a broker charges.
chapters.outcome: You can open a demat and trading account and say which account holds your shares and which holds your cash.
chapters.hook: Your shares never sit with your broker. So where do they actually live?

chapters.title: Placing your first order
chapters.covers: Market order (buy now at any price) versus limit order (buy only at your price or better), choosing quantity, T+1 settlement meaning shares land the next working day, and the charges on one trade.
chapters.outcome: You can buy 1 share with a limit order, say when it lands in your demat, and list the charges you paid.
chapters.hook: A ₹3,000 share can be cheaper than a ₹50 one. One number shows you how.

chapters.title: Reading a shop in five numbers
chapters.covers: Price, market cap (price times all shares, so the size of the shop), P/E (price divided by yearly profit per share, so how many years of profit you pay for), 52-week high and low, and dividend yield.
chapters.outcome: You can look at a quote page and say whether a company is large or small, and whether it is priced high or low against its profit.
chapters.hook: Most paid fund managers fail to beat a plain list of 50 companies over ten years.

chapters.title: Buying the whole bazaar at once
chapters.covers: Index funds buy all 50 Nifty shops in one go; mutual funds hire a shopper to pick for you; SIP means a fixed amount every month; expense ratio is the yearly fee taken from your money.
chapters.outcome: You can set up a monthly SIP in a Nifty 50 index fund and say what expense ratio you are paying.
chapters.hook: 9 in 10 people who trade options in India lose money. SEBI counted.

chapters.title: The toll on the way out, and the traps
chapters.covers: Tax on listed shares: held under 12 months is taxed at 20%, held over 12 months at 12.5% on gains above ₹1.25 lakh a year; why to refuse stock tips, and why SEBI's 2023 study found 9 in 10 individual futures and options traders lost money.
chapters.outcome: You can work out the tax on a sale you are planning and name three things you will say no to in your first year.
chapters.hook: Hold a share 13 months instead of 11 and the tax bill falls. Here is the maths.

picture.name: The town bazaar
picture.line: Think of the stock market as a big town bazaar where you buy tiny slices of the shops themselves, not the goods they sell.

chapters.title: What you actually own when you buy a share
chapters.covers: A share is one slice of a company. Why a company sells slices, what the slice gives you (a vote and a cut of profits), and why its price moves every minute: more buyers than sellers today, or the reverse.
chapters.outcome: You can explain what you own after buying one share of a company and why its price changed today.
chapters.hook: Buy one share and you legally own a sliver of a company. What exactly did you buy?

chapters.title: The bazaar: NSE, BSE, SEBI and the two scoreboards
chapters.covers: India has two big marketplaces, NSE and BSE, open 9:15 am to 3:30 pm on weekdays. SEBI is the inspector who sets the rules. Nifty 50 and Sensex are scoreboards of 50 and 30 big companies, not the whole market.
chapters.outcome: You can read 'Nifty closed 0.8% down' and say which companies that covers, who runs the market, and who polices it.
chapters.hook: The Sensex is just 30 companies. So why does the whole country watch it?

chapters.title: Getting through the gate: broker, Demat and your first order
chapters.covers: Three accounts linked together: bank, trading (where you place orders) and Demat (the locker where shares sit, held by NSDL or CDSL, not your broker). KYC in plain steps, what a market and a limit order are, and why your shares arrive the next day (T+1).
chapters.outcome: You can open the accounts and place a small buy order knowing exactly where the shares land and when.
chapters.hook: Your shares never sit with your broker. So where do they actually live?

chapters.title: Sizing up one shop: five numbers to look at
chapters.covers: Market cap (the whole shop's price; large cap is the top 100 companies, mid cap 101 to 250, small cap the rest), revenue, profit, debt, and the price-to-earnings ratio, which is years of profit you pay for one share. Where to find each on the exchange site and in the annual report.
chapters.outcome: You can look up five numbers on any listed company and say whether it is big, pricey or heavily in debt.
chapters.hook: A ₹3,000 share can be cheaper than a ₹50 one. One number shows you how.

chapters.title: Hiring a shopper: mutual funds, index funds and SIPs
chapters.covers: Pooling money with others and paying a manager (a mutual fund), or just buying the whole Nifty 50 list (an index fund). The expense ratio, which is the yearly fee taken from your money. A SIP, a fixed amount every month, and why most beginners start here.
chapters.outcome: You can choose between an index fund and a stock-picking fund, say what each costs per year, and set up a monthly SIP.
chapters.hook: Most paid fund managers fail to beat a plain list of 50 companies over ten years.

chapters.title: How first-year investors lose money, and how not to
chapters.covers: The four common traps: hot tips, penny stocks, borrowing to trade, and futures and options (bets on where a price goes, where SEBI found roughly 9 in 10 individual traders lose). What a normal 10% to 20% dip looks like and why spreading money across companies softens it.
chapters.outcome: You can name the four common ways beginners lose money in their first year and say which rule protects you from each.
chapters.hook: 9 in 10 people who trade options in India lose money. SEBI counted.

chapters.title: Tax, and your one-page plan
chapters.covers: Sell within 12 months and gains are taxed at 20%; hold longer and it is 12.5% after the first ₹1.25 lakh a year is tax-free. Dividends are taxed as income. Then the plan: emergency fund first, a monthly amount, where it goes, and a yearly review date.
chapters.outcome: You can write a one-page plan that says how much you invest monthly, into what, and what tax you will owe when you sell.
chapters.hook: Hold a share 13 months instead of 11 and the tax bill falls. Here is the maths.
